judgments.proposition: Anita Anant Sawant, the landlady and sole respondent, instituted a Section 6 possession suit against the contesting defendants and the original seller, defendant no. 4.
judgments.quote: the sole respondent filed a suit for possession

judgments.proposition: The plaintiff alleged that she purchased House No. 97 from defendant no. 4 by a registered sale deed dated 1 October 1981 and subsequently obtained possession of the entire house.
judgments.quote: The plaintiff averred in the plaint that she purchased the entire house No. 97
judgments.gap: The reported pleading does not by itself establish good title.

judgments.proposition: The plaintiff alleged that she let the disputed part of the house to P.V. Warik, the tenant.
judgments.quote: she let out southern side one room
judgments.gap: The tenant is identified in the pleading; the excerpt does not reproduce a lease instrument or its terms.

judgments.proposition: The plaintiff alleged that on 1 October 1988 the contesting defendants forcibly ousted tenant P.V. Warik and took the suit property.
judgments.quote: the contesting defendants forcibly dispossessed the tenant
judgments.gap: The pleading is independently evaluated in the trial-court finding recorded below.

judgments.proposition: The contesting defendants claimed that the property was joint-family property, the seller lacked authority, and they were co-owners already in possession.
judgments.quote: suit property was joint family property and defendant no. 4 had no authority
judgments.gap: These are disputed ownership assertions, not findings resolving title.

judgments.proposition: Defendant no. 4 alleged that no consideration was paid and that the sale deed was procured by fraud.
judgments.quote: no consideration was paid to her for the sale of house No. 97
judgments.gap: The judgment does not adjudicate the fraud or consideration allegation in the Section 6 analysis.

judgments.proposition: The trial court found dispossession on 1 October 1988 proved and held that the landlady could sue because she possessed the suit property through the tenant.
judgments.quote: she could maintain the suit
judgments.gap: The Supreme Court recounts the trial finding, not a separate retrial of the factual evidence.

judgments.proposition: The trial court decreed handover of the suit property to the plaintiff on 31 July 2001.
judgments.quote: directed the contesting defendants to handover the possession of the suit property to the plaintiff

judgments.proposition: In revision, the contesting defendants argued that only the dispossessed tenant, not the landlady, could sue under Section 6.
judgments.quote: the tenant and not by the landlady

judgments.proposition: The Bombay High Court rejected the exclusive-tenant-standing argument, holding that either the dispossessed tenant or the landlady could file suit, and dismissed revision on 28 March 2008.
judgments.quote: either the tenant who was actually dispossessed or the plaintiff being landlady could file the suit

judgments.proposition: Section 6(1) allows one dispossessed without consent and outside due process, or anyone claiming through that person, to sue for possession notwithstanding adverse title claims.
objects: otherwise than due course of law
judgments.stage: Statute quoted in Supreme Court judgment
judgments.quote: he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof
judgments.gap: The statutory elements are quoted; case-specific filing timeliness is not established in the judgment.

judgments.proposition: Section 6(2) prohibits a Section 6 suit after six months from dispossession and prohibits such a suit against the Government.
judgments.stage: Statute quoted in Supreme Court judgment
judgments.quote: after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession
judgments.gap: No filing date is supplied for testing the six-month bar in this case.

judgments.proposition: Section 6(3) disallows an appeal or review from an order or decree in a suit instituted under Section 6.
judgments.stage: Statute quoted in Supreme Court judgment
judgments.quote: No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section
judgments.gap: The record describes a High Court revision and a Supreme Court appeal by special leave, not an ordinary statutory appeal from the Section 6 decree.

judgments.proposition: Section 6(4) preserves a separate action to establish title and recover possession.
judgments.stage: Statute quoted in Supreme Court judgment
judgments.quote: Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title
judgments.gap: The competing co-ownership and fraud allegations are not resolved by this summary-possession rationale.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court treated the operative language of Section 6(1) of the 1963 Act and the first paragraph of Section 9 of the 1877 Act as identical when considering the reported precedents.
judgments.quote: "dispossessed" and "he or any person claiming through him"
judgments.gap: Older High Court rulings interpret Section 9 of the repealed 1877 Act; their status is reported authority, not the final Section 6 holding.

judgments.proposition: In Veeraswami Mudali, a Madras High Court single judge took the restrictive position that a landlord lacking an immediate right to physical enjoyment could not evict a trespasser under Section 9.
judgments.quote: so long as landlord did not himself possess the right to enjoy physical possession
judgments.gap: This is a reported precedent expressly rejected by the Supreme Court, not controlling law in the target disposition.

judgments.proposition: In Ramchandra v. Sambashiv, the Nagpur Judicial Commissioners held that the landlord could not sue under Section 9 because the landlord personally had not possessed or been dispossessed.
judgments.quote: a landlord cannot sue under Section 9 to recover possession of the land
judgments.gap: The Supreme Court expressly disapproved this reasoning.

judgments.proposition: In (Kanneganti) Ramamanemma, a Madras High Court single judge held a landlord suit under Section 9 not maintainable without the tenant in possession joined.
judgments.quote: the tenant in possession had not joined, is not maintainable
judgments.gap: This categorical joinder rule is expressly disapproved by the Supreme Court.

judgments.proposition: Nobin Das (Calcutta) reasoned that granting physical occupation to tenants changes the mode of the landlord’s possession, so a forcible tenant eviction can also dispossess the landlord.
judgments.quote: the mode in which he held possession of the property was altered
judgments.gap: That reported case also noted a tenant relinquishment after eviction; the target Supreme Court adopted its possession reasoning without requiring proof of relinquishment here.

judgments.proposition: Ratanlal Ghelabhai (Bombay) distinguished physical tenant occupation from landlord possession and recognized an independent landlord suit for injury to the reversion.
judgments.quote: for an injury to the reversion, the landlord can sue in his own name
judgments.gap: The earlier case distinguished suing in a tenant’s name on immediate possessory rights from an action in the landlord’s own name for injury to reversion.

judgments.proposition: Gobind Ram Jamna Dass (Pepsu) treated the tenant’s possession as the landlord’s and reasoned that denying suit where a tenant refuses to sue would advantage the trespasser and defeat speedy relief.
judgments.quote: a suit is competent by the landlord, even if he is not in actual physical possession
judgments.gap: The tenant-refusal scenario is a policy illustration in the reported precedent, not a found fact about P.V. Warik.

judgments.proposition: Raghuvar Dayal (Rajasthan) approved landlord standing, viewed joining the tenant as proper, and allowed the tenant to join as plaintiff or be impleaded as defendant if unwilling.
judgments.quote: Of course it would be proper to make the tenant also a party to the suit.
judgments.gap: The reported Rajasthan facts involved collusion and a compromise decree, unlike the recorded allegations in the target case.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court distinguished actual physical possession from legal or constructive possession and held that the right to possession can support legal possession for relevant remedial purposes.
judgments.quote: such deprivation may be of actual possession or legal possession
judgments.gap: Halsbury and Pollock and Wright are explanatory sources quoted within the judgment, not separate judicial opinions.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court held that letting property to an exclusive tenant leaves the landlord with legal or constructive possession and legal remedies.
judgments.quote: A landlord by letting out the property to a tenant does not lose possession

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court reasoned that a third party’s unlawful eviction of the tenant dispossesses the landlord in law and gives the landlord an implied right of entry to recover for self and tenant.
judgments.quote: the dispossession of tenant by a third party is dispossession of the landlord

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court read “any person claiming through him” to cover a landlord retaining legal possession through the tenant, permitting the landlord to bring Section 6 proceedings in the landlord’s own name.
judgments.quote: a landlord who holds the possession through his tenant is competent to maintain suit
judgments.gap: This is a rule about standing for immediate possessory recovery, not a determination of ultimate title or entitlement to defeat the tenant’s rights.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court approved the Calcutta possession rationale and the Bombay, Patna, Pepsu and Rajasthan approaches while rejecting the contrary Madras and Nagpur views.
judgments.stage: Supreme Court resolution of precedent conflict (2010)
judgments.quote: The views expressed by Madras High Court in Veeraswami Mudali1
judgments.gap: This record contains one Supreme Court judgment by R.M. Lodha J., signed also by P. Sathasivam J.; it reports no distinct separate judicial opinion.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court held that joining the tenant may be desirable but is not invariably required: a tenant could be uninterested, absent or unwilling to litigate, and non-joinder does not defeat a landlord’s Section 6 suit.
judgments.quote: his non-impleadment is not fatal to the maintainability
judgments.gap: The decision does not say joinder can never be required under any other procedural or factual conditions.

judgments.proposition: The Supreme Court dismissed the contesting defendants’ appeal by special leave without costs, leaving the recovery decree intact.
judgments.quote: appeal fails and is dismissed with no order as to costs
judgments.gap: Disposition is the result, not an independent premise that title, limitation, or factual tenancy details were proved.

judgments.proposition: The original Section 6 suit was filed within six months after the alleged dispossession on 1 October 1988.
judgments.gap: The judgment states a dispossession date, trial decree date, and six-month rule, but never supplies the original filing date; the trial-decree date cannot substitute for it.

decisive_counterarguments: The contesting defendants argued that the tenant alone could invoke Section 6 because the tenant, not the landlady, was physically dispossessed (IK-161859415:L80); this corresponds to the rejected physical-possession-only position of Veeraswami Mudali and Ramchandra (IK-161859415:L101, L103, L156).

The Madras ruling in (Kanneganti) Ramamanemma treated absence of the tenant as fatal to maintainability (IK-161859415:L104). The Supreme Court rejected that categorical rule while acknowledging that joinder may be desirable (IK-161859415:L157-L159).

The contesting defendants claimed joint-family ownership, co-ownership, and the seller’s lack of authority; defendant no. 4 separately alleged fraud and no consideration (IK-161859415:L74). These were title or validity disputes, whereas Section 6(1) permits possessory relief notwithstanding competing title and Section 6(4) preserves title litigation (IK-161859415:L84, L93).

An objection concerning the dispossessed tenant’s interests remains conceptually relevant: the Rajasthan report said it would be proper to join the tenant and allow a say in the relief (IK-161859415:L134-L136). The Supreme Court ruled only that non-joinder is not invariably fatal, not that the tenant’s subsisting interests can always be ignored (IK-161859415:L158-L159).

The statute bars suits brought later than six months after dispossession (IK-161859415:L88), but no initial filing date is provided; the 2001 trial-decree date cannot establish compliance or violation. The reported judgment does not separately resolve that possible procedural issue.
conclusion_boundary: As a source-grounded model reference, the decisive holding is that a landlord retaining legal or constructive possession through an exclusive tenant may invoke Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 against a third-party forcible dispossessor: deprivation of the tenant’s physical occupation also deprives the landlord of legally protected possession, and “any person claiming through him” is not limited to the person physically expelled (IK-161859415:L140-L155). Tenant joinder is potentially desirable but not a universal precondition, particularly where the tenant is unavailable, uninterested, or unwilling to litigate (IK-161859415:L157-L159). This reasoning supports the judgment’s dismissal of the appeal (IK-161859415:L160), not vice versa. The Supreme Court judgment is presented as R.M. Lodha J.’s opinion, signed with P. Sathasivam J., with no separate concurrence or dissent supplied (IK-161859415:L66, L162). The Supreme Court characterized the title issue framed at trial as unnecessary (IK-161859415:L75). The record does not determine ultimate title, sale-deed validity, present tenant wishes, or the original suit’s filing date; the separate title remedy and statutory six-month and government-defendant restrictions remain as quoted (IK-161859415:L74, L84-L93). The statutory no-appeal/no-review provision is distinct from the recorded revision and appeal by special leave (IK-161859415:L79-L81, L91). This is not human gold, legal approval, outcome prediction, or a license to apply this holding beyond the record.
